blocks.body:
Euler showed that $\sum_p 1/p$ diverges, but divergence says nothing about speed. Sieving raises a related question. Strike out every multiple of every prime up to $x$. Each prime $p$ removes about a fraction $1/p$ of what is left, so roughly a fraction $\prod_{p\le x}(1-1/p)$ of the integers should survive. How big is that product?

In 1874 Franz Mertens answered both questions with three estimates. They use nothing deeper than Chebyshev's bound $\psi(x)=O(x)$ from [[chebyshev]]. They are weaker than the prime number theorem, because they average over primes with weights $1/p$, but they are completely elementary, and sieve theory starts from them.

blocks.title: Counting primes inside n!
blocks.body:
Everything starts from the factorisation of $n!$. The exponent of a prime $p$ in $n!$ is $\lfloor n/p\rfloor+\lfloor n/p^2\rfloor+\cdots$: the multiples of $p$ up to $n$ each contribute one factor, the multiples of $p^2$ one more, and so on. Taking logarithms and remembering that the von Mangoldt function has $\Lambda(p^k)=\log p$, we get the exact identity

$$\log n! \;=\; \sum_{p^k\le n}\Big\lfloor \frac{n}{p^k}\Big\rfloor \log p \;=\; \sum_{m\le n}\Lambda(m)\Big\lfloor\frac nm\Big\rfloor .$$

For example $10! = 2^8\cdot 3^4\cdot 5^2\cdot 7$, and indeed $\lfloor 10/2\rfloor+\lfloor 10/4\rfloor+\lfloor 10/8\rfloor = 5+2+1 = 8$.

The left side is easy to estimate. Since $\log t$ is increasing, comparing $\sum_{m=2}^{n}\log m$ and $\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}\log m$ with $\int_1^n\log t\,dt = n\log n-n+1$ gives

$$n\log n - n + 1 \;\le\; \log n! \;\le\; n\log n - n + 1 + \log n .$$

So $\log n!/n = \log n - 1 + O(\log n/n)$. The right side of the identity is almost $n\sum_{m\le n}\Lambda(m)/m$, because replacing $\lfloor n/m\rfloor$ by $n/m$ costs less than $1$ per term, so less than $\sum_{m\le n}\Lambda(m)=\psi(n)$ in total. Chebyshev's bound says exactly that this loss is $O(n)$.

blocks.title: Mertens' first theorem
blocks.body:
For $x\ge 2$,
$$\sum_{n\le x}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n} = \log x + O(1) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sum_{p\le x}\frac{\log p}{p} = \log x + O(1).$$

blocks.title: Proof of the first theorem
blocks.body:
Let $N=\lfloor x\rfloor$. Write $\lfloor N/m\rfloor = N/m - \{N/m\}$ with $0\le\{N/m\}<1$. The identity above becomes
$$\log N! = N\sum_{m\le N}\frac{\Lambda(m)}{m} - E,\qquad 0\le E\le \sum_{m\le N}\Lambda(m)=\psi(N).$$
Divide by $N$. Then $$\sum_{m\le N}\Lambda(m)/m = \log N!/N + E/N = \log N - 1 + O(\log N/N) + O(1)$$, because $E/N\le\psi(N)/N$ is bounded by Chebyshev. Since $\log N = \log x + O(1/x)$, the first statement follows.

For the second, the two sums differ by the prime powers $p^k$ with $k\ge 2$:
$$0\le \sum_{n\le x}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{n}-\sum_{p\le x}\frac{\log p}{p}\le \sum_p\log p\sum_{k\ge2}\frac1{p^k} = \sum_p\frac{\log p}{p(p-1)},$$
and the last series converges (compare with $\sum_n \log n/n^{3/2}$, say). So the difference is bounded.

blocks.title: From weighted sums to the sum of 1/p
blocks.body:
The first theorem counts primes with weight $\log p/p$. To remove the $\log p$, use [[partial-summation]]. Write $A(t)=\sum_{p\le t}\log p/p = \log t + R(t)$, where $|R(t)|\le C$ for $t\ge2$ and $A(t)=0$ for $t<2$. With $f(t)=1/\log t$, so $f'(t)=-1/(t\log^2 t)$, Abel summation gives

$$\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p=\sum_{p\le x}\frac{\log p}{p}\cdot\frac{1}{\log p} = \frac{A(x)}{\log x}+\int_2^x\frac{A(t)}{t\log^2 t}\,dt .$$

Insert $A=\log t+R$. The main part is $1+\int_2^x\frac{dt}{t\log t} = 1+\log\log x-\log\log 2$. The rest is $R(x)/\log x$ plus $\int_2^x R(t)\,dt/(t\log^2t)$. That integral converges as $x\to\infty$, because $\int_2^\infty dt/(t\log^2 t)=1/\log 2$, and its tail beyond $x$ is at most $C/\log x$. Collecting the constants gives the second theorem.

blocks.title: Mertens' second theorem
blocks.body:
There is a constant $M = 0.2614972\ldots$ (the Meissel–Mertens constant) such that for $x\ge2$
$$\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p = \log\log x + M + O\Big(\frac{1}{\log x}\Big).$$
Explicitly $M = 1-\log\log 2+\int_2^\infty R(t)\,\frac{dt}{t\log^2 t}$, with $R$ as above.

blocks.title: The product and the appearance of Euler's constant
blocks.body:
Taking logarithms turns the product into a sum:
$$\log\prod_{p\le x}\Big(1-\frac1p\Big) = -\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p-\sum_{p\le x}h(p),\qquad h(p) = -\log\Big(1-\frac1p\Big)-\frac1p=\sum_{k\ge2}\frac{1}{kp^k}.$$
Since $0<h(p)\le \frac{1}{2p(p-1)}$, the series $H=\sum_p h(p)$ converges, with tail $O(1/x)$. With the second theorem this gives
$$\prod_{p\le x}\Big(1-\frac1p\Big) = \frac{e^{-(M+H)}}{\log x}\Big(1+O\Big(\frac1{\log x}\Big)\Big).$$
That much is routine. The surprise is the value of the constant: $M+H=\gamma$, Euler's constant $0.5772\ldots$. Numerically $H = 0.3157184\ldots$ and $M = 0.2614972\ldots$, which do add up to $\gamma$. Equivalently $M=\gamma+\sum_p\big(\log(1-1/p)+1/p\big)$.

blocks.title: Why the constant is gamma
blocks.body:
We have to show $M+H=\gamma$. The idea is to compute $\log\zeta(1+\delta)$ as $\delta\to0^+$ in two ways. Only one fact about $\zeta$ is needed, and it is elementary: comparing $\sum n^{-1-\delta}$ with $\int_1^\infty t^{-1-\delta}dt = 1/\delta$ gives $1/\delta\le\zeta(1+\delta)\le 1/\delta+1$, so $\log\zeta(1+\delta) = -\log\delta+O(\delta)$.

First way, from the Euler product: $\log\zeta(1+\delta)=\sum_p p^{-1-\delta}+\sum_p h_\delta(p)$ with $h_\delta(p) = -\log(1-p^{-1-\delta})-p^{-1-\delta}$. As $\delta\to0$, $\sum_p h_\delta(p)\to H$ by dominated convergence, since $0\le h_\delta(p)\le h(p)$.

Second way: let $S(t)=\sum_{p\le t}1/p=\log\log t+M+r(t)$ with $r(t)=O(1/\log t)$. Integrating by parts,
$$\sum_p p^{-1-\delta} = \int_{2^-}^\infty t^{-\delta}\,dS(t)=\delta\int_2^\infty S(t)\,t^{-\delta-1}\,dt .$$
Substitute $u=\delta\log t$, so that $t^{-\delta}=e^{-u}$ and $dt/t = du/\delta$. The main part becomes
$$\int_{\delta\log2}^\infty\big(\log u-\log\delta+M\big)e^{-u}\,du = -\gamma-\log\delta+M+o(1),$$
using $\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\log u\,du=\Gamma'(1)=-\gamma$ (see [[gamma]]). The part coming from $r$ is $\int r\,e^{-u}du$ with $|r|\ll\delta/u$. This is $O(\delta\log(1/\delta))$ on $u\le1$ and $O(\delta)$ on $u\ge 1$, so it tends to $0$.

Comparing the two ways: $$-\log\delta+o(1) = (-\log\delta+M-\gamma)+H+o(1)$$, so $M+H=\gamma$.

blocks.title: Checking the three theorems at one million
blocks.body: Compute the three Mertens quantities for $x=10^6$ and compare them with the predictions.
blocks.solution:
There are $78498$ primes up to $10^6$. Summing over them:

1. $\sum_{p\le x}1/p = 2.887328\ldots$, while $\log\log x+M = 2.887289\ldots$. The difference is about $4\times10^{-5}$, much smaller than the guaranteed $O(1/\log x)$.

2. $\log x\cdot\prod_{p\le x}(1-1/p) = 0.561438\ldots$, while $e^{-\gamma}=0.561459\ldots$.

3. $\sum_{p\le x}\log p/p-\log x = -1.3319\ldots$. The first theorem only promises that this is bounded. It does tend to a limit, $-\gamma-\sum_p \log p/(p(p-1)) = -1.33258\ldots$, but showing that the limit exists is about as deep as the prime number theorem; Chebyshev's bounds are not enough.

Note how well the predictions for $\sum 1/p$ and for the product already hold at this modest height.

blocks.title: How many prime factors does a typical integer have?
blocks.body: Let $\omega(n)$ be the number of distinct primes dividing $n$. Show that the average of $\omega(n)$ over $n\le x$ is $\log\log x+M+O(1/\log x)$.
blocks.solution:
Swap the order of summation. Each prime $p\le x$ divides exactly $\lfloor x/p\rfloor$ integers $n\le x$, so
$$\frac1x\sum_{n\le x}\omega(n) = \frac1x\sum_{p\le x}\Big\lfloor\frac xp\Big\rfloor = \sum_{p\le x}\frac1p-\frac1x\sum_{p\le x}\Big\{\frac xp\Big\}.$$
The last term lies between $0$ and $\pi(x)/x$, which is $O(1/\log x)$ by Chebyshev. The second theorem finishes the proof.

At $x=10^6$ the average is $2.8537\ldots$, against $\log\log x+M=2.8873\ldots$. A typical number near a million has only about three distinct prime factors, and this number grows extremely slowly. Hardy and Ramanujan showed that most $n$ have close to $\log\log n$ prime factors. That is the start of [[probabilistic-nt]].

blocks.title: An elementary lower bound
blocks.body:
Without using any of the theorems above, prove that for every $x\ge2$
$$\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p > \log\log x-\frac12 .$$
blocks.solution:
Expand each factor as a geometric series: $(1-1/p)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}p^{-k}$. Multiplying these for $p\le x$ gives a sum of $1/n$ over all $n$ whose prime factors are all at most $x$. This includes every $n\le x$, so
$$\prod_{p\le x}\Big(1-\frac1p\Big)^{-1}\ \ge\ \sum_{n\le x}\frac1n\ >\ \int_1^{\lfloor x\rfloor+1}\frac{dt}{t}\ >\ \log x .$$
Take logarithms: $\sum_{p\le x}-\log(1-1/p)>\log\log x$.

Now we need an upper bound for $-\log(1-u)$. Let $f(u)=u+u^2+\log(1-u)$. Then $f(0)=0$ and $f'(u) = \dfrac{u(1-2u)}{1-u}\ge0$ on $[0,\tfrac12]$, so $-\log(1-u)\le u+u^2$ there. With $u=1/p$:
$$\sum_{p\le x}\frac1p + \sum_p\frac1{p^2} > \log\log x .$$
Finally, $\sum_p 1/p^2\le \frac14+\sum_{n\ge3,\ n \text{ odd}}\frac1{n^2} = \frac14+\frac{\pi^2}8-1<0.484<\frac12$. (The true value is $0.4522\ldots$.) Hence $\sum_{p\le x}1/p>\log\log x-\sum_p1/p^2>\log\log x-\tfrac12$.

blocks.title: Where the sieve heuristic breaks
blocks.body: How many integers $n\le N=10^6$ have no prime factor $\le 1000$? Compare the answer with the heuristic $N\prod_{p\le1000}(1-1/p)$.
blocks.solution:
Since $1000=\sqrt N$, an integer $n\le N$ with no prime factor up to $1000$ is either $1$ or a prime in $(1000,N]$. The count is therefore exactly $1+\pi(10^6)-\pi(1000) = 1+78498-168 = 78331$.

The heuristic gives $10^6\prod_{p\le1000}(1-1/p) = 80965.3\ldots$, about $3\%$ too large. As $N\to\infty$ the error does not go away. By Mertens the heuristic is asymptotic to $e^{-\gamma}N/\log\sqrt N = 2e^{-\gamma}N/\log N$, while the prime number theorem says the true count is asymptotic to $N/\log N$. The ratio tends to $2e^{-\gamma}=1.1229\ldots$.

The reason is that the events "$p\mid n$" for different primes are only approximately independent. Write $z$ for the sieving limit (here $z=1000$). The small errors from the individual primes accumulate when $z$ is as large as $\sqrt N$, and the heuristic $N\prod_{p\le z}(1-1/p)$ is asymptotically right only when $\log z$ is small compared with $\log N$. Controlling this error is the business of [[sieve-basics]].

blocks.body:
- The constant in $\sum 1/p$ is $M\approx0.2615$, not $\gamma$. Euler's constant enters only in the product, through the extra convergent sum $H$.
- $\prod_{p\le z}(1-1/p)$ is the density of integers free of primes up to $z$ only when $z$ is small compared with $N$. At $z=\sqrt N$ it overestimates by the factor $2e^{-\gamma}$ (see the last example).
- The first theorem gives $O(1)$, not $\log x + C + o(1)$. The limit does exist, but proving that is about as deep as the prime number theorem.
- $\log$ is the natural logarithm throughout. With $\log_{10}$, all the constants change.
- Mertens' theorems do not imply $\pi(x)\sim x/\log x$. Averaging with weight $1/p$ washes out exactly the information the prime number theorem needs.

Mertens' product $V(z)=\prod_{p< z}(1-1/p)$ is the main term in every sieve, from Eratosthenes–Legendre through Brun and Selberg ([[sieve-basics]], [[selberg-sieve]]). Its size $e^{-\gamma}/\log z$ is why sieve upper bounds for twin primes and similar problems come out of order $x/\log^2x$.

The second theorem is used repeatedly for sums like $\sum_{y<p\le x}1/p = \log(\log x/\log y)+o(1)$. These sums are central in the study of [[primitive-sets]], where Erdős's sum $\sum 1/(a\log a)$ is compared with the corresponding sum over primes. They also drive the Hardy–Ramanujan and Erdős–Kac theorems in [[probabilistic-nt]]. The same partial-summation argument, run with the full [[pnt]] in place of Chebyshev's bound, gives sharper error terms.

1. Show that $\sum_{\sqrt x<p\le x}1/p\to\log 2$. Deduce that the number of $n\le x$ having a prime factor greater than $\sqrt x$ is asymptotic to $x\log 2$. (Each such $n$ has only one such prime factor.)
2. Show that $\prod_{p\le x}(1-1/p^2)$ converges to a positive limit, while $\prod_{p\le x}(1-1/p)\to0$. Identify the first limit.
3. Let $P=\prod_{p\le x}p$. Using the third theorem and Chebyshev's bound $\theta(x)\le Cx$, show that $P/\varphi(P)\ge c\log\log P$ for large $x$, for some constant $c>0$.
4. In the proof of the first theorem, which of the two inequalities $\sum_{m\le N}\Lambda(m)/m\ge\log N-C$ and $\sum_{m\le N}\Lambda(m)/m\le\log N+C$ uses Chebyshev's bound, and which needs no information about primes at all?
